https://www.dw.com/en/deceived-and-deplo.text: Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites https://p.dw.com/p/5JQsq Young men across Africa are being tricked into leaving their home countries to fight in Russia's war Image: Isaac Kaledzi/DW Advertisement Cameroon has emerged as one of the leading sources of African recruits for the Russian military , with young men lured to Europe by false promises of jobs and fast-tracked Russian citizenship, only to find themselves on the front lines of the war in Ukraine. As of May this year, Ukrainian officials say that nearly 3,000 citizens from various African countries were known to have fought — or to still be fighting — for Russia : Cameroon, Ghana, Egypt, Kenya and Uganda were identified as significant. In April, the Cameroonian government confirmed that Russia had reported the deaths of 16 Cameroonian nationals, seven of whom had died in military action in Ukraine. Charles Ojiambo Mutoka, 72, shows a picture of his son Oscar, who he learned was killed while fighting for Russia in Ukraine Image: Tony Karumba/AFP Poverty driving youths into Russia's duplicitous schemes The actual death toll is likely higher according to DW correspondent Dorcas Ekupe, reporting from Bamenda in northwestern Cameroon. "When you look at other publications and see what is happening — even seeing families who are grieving their loved ones — the number is really much higher than what the government had earlier said," Ekupe told DW's AfricaLink program. She described two forces causing this worrying phenomenon: economic desperation and deliberate deception. Many recruits, she said, travelled to Russia believing they had secured jobs in construction or as security guards, or that they were participating in study programs. "Once in Russia, they then end up on the battlefield," Ekupe said. African recruits fighting in Ukraine: Where's the AU? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video Russia's perceived appeal meanwhile is also being amplified by well-organized campaigns. Banjo Herman, a lecturer and political analyst at the University of Bamenda, pointed to the key role of the the Russian paramilitary Wagner Group as well as its successor, the Africa Corps, as Moscow's primary instrument for expanding its presence and reputation across Africa. Military recruitment dressed up as 'cultural' outreach Herman also cited Russian government programs such as the African Initiative and Alabuga, which present themselves as cultural or educational exchange schemes but have been linked to military recruitment. "On the surface, sometimes it looks like cultural outreach," he said. "Sometimes Cameroonians are lured, thinking it is for work, not necessarily knowing what is beneath the surfac.," He added that offers of Russian nationality within six months were a particularly powerful draw. France has previously described the African Initiative as a front administered by Russian intelligence services, designed to spread propaganda. Why young men continue to risk their lives Herman stressed, however, that the economic situation of the men was typically the main motivator . "Imagine that you are a carpenter in Cameroon who cannot even earn 100,000 CFA francs (€150; $175) a month, but somebody is promising you 3 million CFA francs to come and work," he explained. "It is very attractive." He also highlighted the fact that not all Cameroonians in Russia were the victims of deception: Some had lived there for years, had been absorbed into the military over time and were doing reasonably well. But he pointed out that it was the promise of financial reward combined with the prospect of gaining Russian citizenship that explained why even people aware of the risks continued to accept recruitment offers to fight in Ukraine . Ekupe corroborated this, noting a prevailing attitude of fatalism among some youth: "Sometimes people say, 'If I die, I die.'" Africans pay high human cost fighting for Russia in Ukraine To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video Those left behind often suffer the most Families left behind, meanwhile, are forced to bear the cost in silence: Ekupe described cases in which mothers only learned of their sons' deaths years after the fact — in one instance, when a fellow soldier called home to report that a 35-year-old Cameroonian had been killed in combat. She added that many families had received no financial compensation from the Cameroonian government and that some of the men who died had left behind pregnant wives as well as children. Contact between recruits and their families is often severed abruptly, Ekupe said. "When they get there and discover it was not as promised, it is really difficult to inform their family," she added. "Sometimes they have to take time to adjust to the new environment and the situation, in which they find themselves." According to the Kenyan Ministry of Foreign Affairs, more than 200 Kenyan nationals had crossed into Russia by January 2026, but only 18 had returned Image: Minako Sasako/AP Photo/picture alliance Russia ducking from responsibilty On the question of legal responsibility, Herman noted that international law does not, in principle, prohibit a foreign national from voluntarily enlisting in another state's armed forces. Legal liability arises, however, when recruitment involves fraud, coercion, trafficking or mercenary activity. Herman cited Article 47 of the Additional Protocol to the Geneva Conventions, which defines a mercenary as someone who agrees to take direct part in hostilities with private financial gain as their main motivation. Under current frameworks, the responsibility for the death of a foreign fighter in another country's war rests largely with the individual and their family, not the recruiting state. Cameroon: insufficient campaigns to fight recruitement Cameroon's government has stated publicly that it does not deploy troops abroad outside international mandates, and has warned citizens against joining foreign conflicts. Analysts have nevertheless called on the Cameroonian government, and African governments more broadly, to pursue a three-pronged response to stop more people from risking their lives in Russia. This approach would include economic reforms to create opportunities and reduce the conditions that make deceptive recruitment attractive; direct diplomatic engagement with Russia to hold recruitment networks accountable; and a public awareness campaign that issues clear, proactive public warnings to citizens about the dangers of following such schemes. Relatives of Kenyan nationals conscripted by the Russian army have demanded government action to repatriate their kin Image: Tony Karumba/AFP Ghana has also formally raised the issue with Russia, demanding an end to the recruitment of its nationals. However, in Cameroon's case, the country's longstanding military ties with Russia, which President Paul Biya moved to renew in 2014 and 2015, could prevent a similar move. Herman said that the absence of an official Cameroonian policy response to date reflected, at least in part, the government's awareness that the recruitment is carried out by private actors — limiting the state's formal grounds and opportunities for intervention. "For the government to stop this," he said, "it has to go back to its governance policy and have a policy that is inclusive, transparent, and in which people can find opportunities within the system." https://www.dw.com/en/poland-says-starli.text: Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites https://p.dw.com/p/5NCMT Starlink stations in Poland help service Ukraine Image: NurPhoto/IMAGO Advertisement Warsaw considers a fire that broke out at a Starlink station in central Poland to be an act of sabotage, Deputy Prime Minister Krzysztof Gawkowski said on Thursday. "This act of sabotage was deliberately designed to disable the station ... disrupting internet access for various institutions, including the Ukrainian army," Gawkowski, who also serves as digital minister, told public broadcaster TVP. He said the fire at the station belonging to Polish state-owned telecom company Exatel broke out late on Wednesday. "There is much to suggest that we are dealing with an element of the next phase of hybrid warfare," he said. The deputy premier said that the station was used to transmit internet traffic through Poland, including to neighboring Ukraine . He also said there were "many indications" suggesting the incident "fits into this new Russian doctrine of attack." Gawkowski warned that the incident could reflect a 'new Russian doctrine of attack' Image: Klaudia Radecka/NurPhoto/picture alliance Poland accuses Russia of 'hybrid' warfare Poland and other EU and NATO member states have accused Russia of engaging in hybrid warfare , including acts of sabotage, against Ukraine's allies, since Moscow launched its full-scale invasion in February 2022 . Lying on the EU and NATO's eastern flank, Poland borders Ukraine, the Russian exclave of Kaliningrad and Moscow ally Belarus. It is one of Kyiv's strongest supporters in Europe . Warsaw also joined the new "Carpathian Eight" regional summit launched by Ukraine last Friday. Earlier in September, Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk warned that Russia plans to carry out "hybrid" drone and missile strikes against Ukraine's allies. Late last year, Poland accused Russia of carrying out "state terrorism" over an act of sabotage on the Polish rail network. Europe Home page Europe 0 0 EU to pay Slovakia €105 million for military equipment donated to Ukraine 29 September 2026 04:20 (UTC +04:00) The European Union will pay Slovakia €105 million in compensation through the European Peace Facility for military equipment donated to Ukraine, APA reports. Robert Bestro, Director General of the Defence Policy Department at Slovakia’s Ministry of Defence, announced the decision. “We have secured another €105 million for Slovakia from the European Peace Facility. These funds are now a reality. The decision was taken this week,” he said. Bestro noted that the funding would be in addition to compensation Slovakia had previously received. Slovakia’s previous government supplied Ukraine with military equipment from 2022, including MiG-29 fighter jets and an S-300 air defense system. The current Slovak government has ended the practice of donating weapons and ammunition to Ukraine. However, Slovak companies are permitted to supply weapons to Ukraine on a commercial basis. Belgium: 9 minors arrested as clashes erupt near Brussels-Midi Copy/paste the link below: Copy Copy/paste the article video embed link below: Copy Updated: 13/10/2026 - 7:55 GMT+2 Clashes near Brussels-Midi station leave around ten arrested, including nine minors, as student and anti-austerity protests continue in Belgium. … More Belgian police arrested ten people, including nine minors , after clashes involving hundreds of young people near Brussels-Midi railway station on Monday, 12 October. Officers reported being targeted with stones and fireworks as unrest broke out on the sidelines of a national strike and a student gathering. ADVERTISEMENT ADVERTISEMENT Police deployed tear gas and water cannon as groups moved between the station, Place Bara and the Cureghem neighbourhood, occasionally dispersing into Anderlecht and Saint-Gilles before returning. The Clemenceau metro station was temporarily closed, while a car, several scooters and street furniture were set alight. Officers also seized fireworks, flammable liquids and aerosol cans. The violence came amid growing protests against austerity measures, rising living costs and education cuts . Since 1 October, secondary-school pupils have been demonstrating against plans to save €500 million from French-speaking education by 2029. Trade unions are also opposing Prime Minister Bart De Wever's proposed €10 billion savings programme . In Liège, more than 200 arrests have been reported since the student protests began. A separate anti-austerity march in Brussels drew around 30,000 people on Friday , according to police, and was also followed by clashes.
